rationale: Instrumenting the appender's own log resolves the last gap, and it resolves it against my defect claim. For seed 35 the appended joint change at index 4 came from node 2 at step 22, and node 2's own log is '1:t0 2:t2(tr=1,1:4) 3:t0 4:t2(tr=1,0:4)' with applied_before=3, pending_conf_index_before=2 and joint_before=false - that is, node 2 had applied three entries of a log whose index 2 is a joint-enter change, yet its tracked configuration was not joint. A node that applies a joint change in order must be joint, so the appender's tracker came from somewhere other than its log, and the harness has exactly such a path: the restart event rebuilds a node with Config.Applied set to its applied index while its tracker is restored from the ConfState the harness writes into storage from the tracker itself, so a node whose applied index already covers a configuration change can come back with a non-joint tracker and, in that state, append a second joint-enter change with both propose-time clauses false. That makes the rejected history an artifact of my restart modelling rather than a state the target can reach through its own producers, so I refute the availability claim for the receipts at hand while keeping the consequence chain (in-order application of a joint-enter change on a joint configuration is rejected and applyConfChange panics) and the documented best-effort nature of the propose-time checks on record as the reasons the path exists at all.

Applying a joint-enter change in log order makes a tracker joint, so the appender's tracked configuration did not come from its own log; the harness's restart event is the path that can produce this, because it rebuilds a node with Config.Applied taken from the node's applied index while the tracker is restored from the ConfState the harness writes into storage, which is taken from the tracker at restart time rather than from the log the applied index covers. Under that modelling a node can return non-joint with an applied index that already includes a configuration change, and in that state both propose-time clauses are false so a second joint-enter change is appended.
knowledge.conditions: Sweep revision with restarts of random nodes, application lag and configuration events; the observation is draft-side and has no controller receipt yet, and it is a statement about the harness's restart modelling rather than about the target's own producers.

interpretations.rationale: The consequence chain recorded from the receipts is unchanged and remains true: applying a joint-enter change on a joint configuration is rejected by the Changer, applyConfChange panics on that error, three nodes applied the rejected history in order with reapplied_entry false, and a JointImplicit change that alters no membership still creates a joint configuration. What is refuted is the reachability that the availability claim needed. Recording the appender's own state shows the appended change came from a node whose log already contained a joint-enter change at index 2, whose applied index was 3, and whose tracker was nevertheless not joint - a tracker that cannot come from its own log, since applying that change in order makes it joint. The harness has exactly one path that produces such a node: the restart event rebuilds a node with Config.Applied from its applied index while restoring the tracker from the ConfState the harness writes into storage, which is taken from the tracker rather than from the log the applied index covers. So the rejected history is a state my restart modelling created, not one the target's own producers produce, and with it the asserted trigger falls: no receipt shows a permitted history in which a leader with an in-order applied log appends a second joint-enter change. The claim narrows to what survives: the propose-time check is best-effort by the target's own documentation with false negatives, the deterministic case shows the guard admitting a second joint-enter change in a hand-supplied stale state, and the apply side panics rather than rejecting the change - which together mark a robustness gap worth a follow-up in a context where a caller does disable or defeat the check, but not an availability defect proved reachable through permitted operations in this snapshot.

knowledge.assertion: the appender of the rejected change had applied 3 entries and a non-joint tracker

counterevidence: The refutation rests on operands from a draft-side run that has no receipt yet, so it is a correction of my own construction rather than a receipt-backed negative; the earlier receipts remain as they were.

The doc-stated false negatives of the propose-time check are real: the check consults leader-local state, so a caller whose configuration stale-ness differs from the leader's, or who sets DisableConfChangeValidation, can still put an invalid change in the log and reach the panic.

The deterministic stale-guard case shows the guard admitting in a state I supplied by hand; that state is reachable only if a leader can hold a non-joint tracker over an applied joint change, which the receipts do not show.
